tagline.text: A hydroelectric dam and reservoir, opened in 1956, closing off a Benguet mountain gorge

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱600–1,500 (day trip from Baguio, including transport, food and activities)

children.text: Ambuklao Dam is a hydroelectric dam in Bokod, Benguet, about 40 km northeast of Baguio, and it opened in 1956. With an emerald-green reservoir on the Agno River and mountain scenery all around, it makes an easy short stop on a day trip.
Ambuklao Dam sits in Barangay Ambuklao, in the municipality of Bokod, Benguet, in the Cordillera highlands of northern Luzon. It is about
36km
in a straight line from central Baguio and about
by road, which usually takes 1.5 to 2 hours by car. Compared with the long journey from Manila to Baguio, it is close, so it often appears on day-trip itineraries based in Baguio.
Construction began in July 1950, and the dam opened on
December 23, 1956
. It was built for power generation and flood control and is a rock-fill embankment dam with a central core. It is about
high and about
long. Some sources give the height as 131 m, so treat the figures as approximate. It was once presented as one of the tallest dams in the world.

The Agno River rises near Mount Data and flows into this gorge. The water held behind the dam formed a reservoir, and as silt and sand built up, its surface area shrank. After the 1990 Luzon earthquake, siltation and equipment problems worsened, and the power plant stopped operating in 1999. In the November 2007 public bid, SN Aboitiz Power-Benguet took over the plant together with the nearby Binga facility, and after rehabilitation work it came back online in 2011. Installed capacity rose from 75 MW to 105 MW. The plant is known to run for short periods when power demand peaks, helping to stabilize the grid.

As a travel destination, Ambuklao Dam is not a place with flashy tourist facilities. You come to see a huge concrete and rock structure set between mountains, with a quiet lake in front of it. There is no entrance fee, and it is open during daylight hours, so it is easy to drop in. However, the plant and dam area are facilities managed by the operating company, so follow the signs and staff instructions, and the areas you may enter can change from time to time. It is best thought of as a quiet stop to slot into a Baguio and Benguet highlands itinerary rather than a major attraction, and that way your expectations will match what you find.

The wall-like dam closing the valley and the lake spreading out behind it fit into a single frame. Guides mention a viewing deck on site, which is a good spot for photos looking down over the whole reservoir. The colors are best in the morning and late afternoon, when the sunlight is low. The steep mountain slopes on both sides of the gorge contrast with the deep green of the lake, so the scene has atmosphere even on overcast days.
Tourism guides list boat rides on the lake from
. However, boat operations have changed over time, and in 2022 the municipality was reported to be pursuing boating as a tourism product. Check whether it is running before you go.

Older visitor accounts describe kayaking on the calm, emerald-colored water. Whether it is still available depends on local conditions, so ask the Bokod tourism office or local residents before your visit.
Tourism guides list fishing from
and sightseeing from
. A Bokod municipal official has said that the upper reaches of the lake are suitable for picnics and camping. Confirm fees and how to use these services on site.

Past visitor accounts describe walking along the dam crest and looking down at the water pouring below. When water is released, the roar and spray are impressive. Access may be restricted for security and safety, so follow staff instructions first.

A festival honoring tilapia farming, the village's main livelihood, is held every March. In 2022 it took place on March 14. The date can change from year to year, so check municipal announcements if you plan to visit.
Bokod's best-known attraction is the 24 km Mount Purgatory trail. It passes through mossy forest and six major peaks, and the highest, Mount Tangbaw, stands at
. Hiking is done in the November–May dry season, and you must register at the municipal hall.

items.title: Day trip from Baguio
items.subtitle: Dam views, lunch and the return

children.text: Leave
Baguio
. If you have your own car or a rental, follow the Benguet–Nueva Vizcaya Road and turn off at the Ambuklao junction. By public transport, take a jeepney or van toward Bokod from the Dangwa terminal.
Stop briefly at a scenic stretch on the way to rest. The mountain road has many curves and car sickness is common, so bring water and snacks before you leave.
Arrive at the dam, photograph the lake and dam from a good viewpoint, and look around the areas you are allowed to walk, following the on-site guidance.
If it is operating, take a boat on the lake or relax near the embankment. Ask on site first whether it is running and what it costs.
Eat lunch at a roadside eatery nearby. There are few restaurants right next to the dam, so roadside snack eateries or a packed lunch are the realistic choices.
If you have time, head toward the Jang-Jang Hanging Bridge area and cross the bridge. It is said to be about
4km
from the dam, but it may take longer depending on road conditions, so confirm locally.
Arrange transport back to Baguio. Public transport back can be infrequent, so move before dark.
If you rely on public transport alone, return vehicles can be rare, so leave plenty of time.

items.title: Two days around Bokod
items.subtitle: The dam, the hanging bridge and Mount Purgatory

children.text: See the dam first and enjoy the view of the lake.
Visit nearby sights such as the Jang-Jang Hanging Bridge or the viewing deck in Bokod town. Agree on the fare with a local driver before you set off.
To take on the Mount Purgatory trail, you must register at the municipal hall and pay the fee. Hiking is recommended only in the November–May dry season.
Bokod has only a few homestays, and no hotel information could be confirmed. Ask the municipal tourism office about lodging in advance, or consider staying in Baguio.
Take a long-distance bus from Manila to Baguio. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so leave some slack in your schedule.
It is easier on your body to sleep one night in Baguio and go to the dam the next day.
From Clark International Airport (CRK) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), continue overland.
Bus companies and timetables change often. Check the latest information.
Board a vehicle toward Bokod or Ambuklao at the Dangwa terminal in Baguio. Some sources also describe boarding at the Slaughter Compound in Magsaysay.
Bokod's local transport route plan lists Baguio–Ambuklao and Bokod routes. Travel times range widely between sources, from about 1.5 hours to several hours.
Fares differ between sources and many are old, so only a range of about ₱100–300 is known. Confirm with the dispatcher before boarding.
Some accounts say return vehicles are rare, so work out your way back before you go.
From Baguio, use the Benguet–Nueva Vizcaya Road and the Ambuklao Road, about
38km
, roughly 1.5 hours.
The mountain road can be slippery in rain or fog, and rockfalls are possible. Plan to be back before dark.
No verified parking information was found, so follow on-site guidance.
You can look around the dam area on foot.
To reach nearby sights, you will need to arrange a local vehicle.

Ambuklao Dam is reached by mountain roads, so the dry season, with less rain, is safer and the views are clearer. November to May is best, and December to February is especially cool and comfortable for walking.
During the June–October rainy season, the risk of rockfalls and landslides rises. If a typhoon is forecast, it is safer to postpone.
For a day trip, arrive in the morning. In the afternoon, clouds and fog often rise between the mountains and block the view, and it also becomes hard to finish the drive back before dark.

There is not much lodging around the dam. Bokod town has only a few homestays, so most travelers stay in Baguio and visit as a day trip. If you need a place to sleep, ask the Bokod tourism office in advance.

Meals center on simple eateries along the Benguet–Nueva Vizcaya Road. Guides say there are almost no restaurants right next to the dam, so bringing a packed lunch and drinking water is convenient. Bokod reportedly has no banks or ATMs, so carry enough cash.

After you return to Baguio, the strawberry farms and cafes in nearby La Trinidad are a good place to rest. Picking up Benguet vegetables, strawberries and coffee is part of the fun of this trip. See also
La Trinidad Strawberry Farm
if you like.
Leaving Baguio early in the morning lets you see the lake in clear light.
Carry plenty of cash. Guides say Bokod has no banks or ATMs.
Return transport can be scarce, so if you use public transport, confirm how you will get back beforehand.
If you want to use a drone or large equipment, ask the on-site staff for permission first.
Bring water, snacks, a hat and sunscreen. There is little shade.
Boat rides, kayaking and fishing may change in availability and price, so check before you visit.
If you get carsick easily, take medicine before leaving. The mountain road has many curves.
When paying fees on site, check whether there is a receipt or a posted price list.
When taking photos, it is polite not to frame plant equipment or staff prominently without permission.
After rain, some stretches see frequent landslides and rockfalls, so avoid visiting in the rainy and typhoon season or postpone your trip.
Mountain roads have stretches with low or no guardrails and thick fog.
The dam and power facilities are controlled areas. Follow signs and staff instructions, and do not enter restricted zones.
Near the lake and spillways, water levels can rise suddenly because of releases. Stay away from the water's edge.
Always wear a life jacket on boats and kayaks.
Hours and access rules can change, so check the latest announcements.
About
1.5–2 hours
away by car. It is easiest to handle lodging, meals and money exchange in Baguio.
The Ambuklao road is known to continue north toward Kabayan and Buguias. To go further into the northern highlands, plan a separate trip. Plan the Kabayan Mummy Caves as their own full-day outing.
Tourism sources mention visiting Ambuklao Dam together with Mount Pulag or Mount Purgatory itineraries. Mount Pulag is a hike that requires a separate permit and a guide.
Bokod's signature trek, 24 km long, passing mossy forest and six peaks. Registration at the municipal hall is required.
A hanging bridge about
4km
from the dam that many visitors combine with the dam. Confirm the exact access route locally.
